legal.cookies.title: Cookie Policy
legal.cookies.body:
Operator: Individual Entrepreneur Dmitrii Tunguskov
Email: info@rabbitmatch.pro
Effective date: 01.01.2026
Last updated: 28.05.2026
URL: https://www.rabbitmatch.pro/legal/cookies

1. What Are Cookies

1.1. Cookies are small text files stored on a User's device when they visit the web version of the Application. In mobile apps and the Telegram Mini App, similar functionality is provided by local storage (localStorage), session storage (sessionStorage), and other tracking technologies.

2. Types of Cookies We Use

| Type               | Purpose                               | Retention              | Consent Required |
| ------------------ | ------------------------------------- | ---------------------- | ---------------- |
| Strictly Necessary | Authentication, security, session     | Session / up to 1 year | No               |
| Functional         | Language, UI preferences              | Up to 1 year           | No               |
| Analytical         | Usage analysis, error tracking        | Up to 2 years          | Yes              |
| Marketing          | Personalized advertising, retargeting | Up to 1 year           | Yes              |

2.1. Strictly Necessary Cookies are used for:
• User authentication and session security;
• Remembering booking progress;
• CSRF token protection.

2.2. Analytical Cookies. We use the following analytics tools: Google Analytics, Amplitude, Mixpanel.

2.3. Marketing Cookies are only used with explicit User consent.

3. Third-Party Cookies

3.1. The Application may use cookies from:
• Telegram — for authentication and Mini App functionality. Policy: https://telegram.org/privacy
• Google (Google Auth, Google Analytics, if applicable)
• Infrastructure services (Railway, Expo) — technical cookies

4. Managing Cookies

4.1. Users may at any time:
• change Cookie preferences in the Application's Cookie Settings Center (if available);
• opt out of analytical and marketing cookies via the Cookie banner;
• clear cookies in the browser settings;
• use browser extensions to block cookies.

4.2. Disabling strictly necessary cookies may prevent use of the Application.

4.3. In Telegram Mini App, localStorage management is handled through Telegram client settings.

5. Legal Basis

5.1. Cookies are processed on the following legal grounds:
• Strictly necessary cookies — legitimate interest of the Operator;
• Analytical and marketing cookies — User consent (GDPR Art. 6(1)(a)).

legal.refund.title: Refund Policy
legal.refund.body:
Operator: Individual Entrepreneur Dmitrii Tunguskov
Email: info@rabbitmatch.pro
Effective date: 01.01.2026
Last updated: 28.05.2026

1. General

1.1. This Refund Policy sets out the conditions and procedure for refunds to RabbitMatch Application Users.

1.2. Refunds are processed in accordance with Georgian law and applicable local consumer protection law based on the User's country of residence.

1.3. The maximum refund amount shall not exceed the total amount actually paid by the User to the Operator in the preceding 12 months.

2. Subscription Refunds

2.1. Trial period. If a User subscribes with a free or discounted trial and cancels within the trial period, no charge is made.

2.2. First payment. A full refund for the first payment is available within 14 days of the charge, provided the User has not accessed paid features.

2.3. Subsequent payments. Refunds for completed billing periods are not provided, except:
• technical failure preventing access to paid features for more than 72 hours continuously due to the Operator's fault;
• discontinuation of the Service by the Operator — pro-rated refund for unused period.

2.4. No refund for violations. Refunds are not issued if a subscription was cancelled due to User breach of the Agreement or other policies.

2.5. App Store / Google Play purchases. For subscriptions purchased via Apple App Store or Google Play, refunds are governed by the respective platform's policies. The Operator does not directly manage the refund process for such purchases.

3. Booking Refunds

3.1. The refund conditions for a court reservation are determined by the policy of the court owners and are implemented by default on their side; in other cases:

| Time Before Start       | Refund Condition             |
| ----------------------- | ---------------------------- |
| More than 48 hours      | Full refund (100%)           |
| 24–48 hours             | Partial refund (50%)         |
| Less than 24 hours      | No refund                    |
| Confirmed force majeure | Individual return conditions |

3.2. The initiator of the cancellation must be the User (not another person accepted for the game). The request is made through the Application or sent to info@rabbitmatch.pro with the subject line "Refund" and a full description of the reason for the refund and the details for the refund.

3.3. If the court is cancelled due to the venue owner's fault or for technical reasons on the Operator's side, a full refund is issued.

4. Refund Request Procedure

4.1. To request a refund, Users email info@rabbitmatch.pro with:
• username / account ID;
• payment date and amount;
• reason for the request;
• proof of payment (screenshot, receipt);
• payment details for the refund.

4.2. The Operator reviews requests within 14 business days and notifies the User of the decision.

4.3. Approved refunds are returned to the original payment method within 30 business days of the decision.

4.4. The Operator is not responsible for refund delays caused by transaction processing times of payment systems or banks.

5. Non-Refundable Cases

Refunds are not issued in the following cases:
• Breach of the Agreement or other policies of the Application;
• Unauthorized advertising;
• Match result manipulation or booking fraud;
• Fraudulent use of the Application;
• Disagreement with updated terms where functionality has not changed;
• Change of the User's personal circumstances;
• Account access loss due to the User's own fault (compromise of credentials).
legal.booking.title: Court Booking Rules
legal.booking.body:
Operator: Individual Entrepreneur Dmitrii Tunguskov
Email: info@rabbitmatch.pro
Effective date: 01.01.2026
Last updated: 28.05.2026

1. Subject Matter

1.1. These Rules govern the booking of sports venues through the RabbitMatch Application.

1.2. The Application acts as an intermediary platform between Users and venue owners. The Operator is not the owner or lessor of courts and is not liable for the physical condition, surface quality, availability of equipment, or other characteristics dependent on the venue owner.

2. Booking Process

2.1. The User selects a venue, date, time, and duration.

2.2. The system checks the availability of the selected slot.

2.3. The User confirms the booking and pays via the Application's payment service.

2.4. After successful payment, the User receives a booking confirmation with a unique order number.

2.5. The booking is confirmed only upon successful payment.

3. Rights and Obligations

3.1. The User must:
• arrive at the court at the booked time;
• comply with venue rules;
• not transfer the booking to third parties without approval;
• notify the Operator of cancellation in accordance with the Refund Policy.

3.2. The Operator may:
• cancel bookings for technical reasons with a full refund;
• suspend booking access for Users who repeatedly violate rules or cancel bookings 2 times per month;
• change booking prices with 12 hours' notice.

3.3. The Operator is not liable for:
• force majeure (weather, venue closure, health restrictions);
• court quality and condition;
• venue owner actions after confirmation;
• injuries or health damage on the premises.

4. Special Conditions

4.1. Uncoordinated advertising at the venue. It is prohibited to use the reserved court for commercial events or promotions without prior approval from the Operator.

4.2. Booking on behalf of an organization. If a User books a court for an event with a commercial component (paid tournaments, sponsored events), the User is obliged to notify the Operator and obtain written consent.

home.audiences.title: Four different people, one app
home.audiences.lead: A player looking for a game. An organizer running a tournament. A coach filling a schedule. A club watching occupancy. Until now that was four group chats, two spreadsheets and one administrator who answers in the evenings.
home.audiences.items.0.title: Players
home.audiences.items.0.text: Open games nearby, already filtered to your level. A rating that moves after every match. And a real breakdown of your own game: which side of the court you are stronger on, when you win more often, how you hold up in deciding sets.
home.audiences.items.1.title: Organizers
home.audiences.items.1.text: From an Americano to a month-long championship. Draws and standings compute themselves, and anything that goes wrong you fix yourself, mid-event, without waiting on support.
home.audiences.items.2.title: Coaches
home.audiences.items.2.text: A profile with prices and specialisations, a schedule students book directly, reviews. The reputation stays yours even if you change clubs.
home.audiences.items.3.title: Venues
home.audiences.items.3.text: Your free hours reach people looking for somewhere to play tonight. Plus a CRM and occupancy analytics.
home.how.title: Five steps and you are on court
home.how.lead: Not one phone call to an administrator.
home.how.items.0.title: Install the app
home.how.items.0.text: iOS, Android, browser or Telegram. Same account everywhere. Through Telegram it takes about thirty seconds — you do not even invent a password.
home.how.items.1.title: Say what you play and where
home.how.items.1.text: Sport, city, rough level. Guess the level: the rating corrects it over your first few matches.
home.how.items.2.title: Take a spot, or create your own game
home.how.items.2.text: The feed shows who is short of people: format, time, venue, spots left. Creating your own takes a minute and puts it in front of everyone who fits the level.
home.how.items.3.title: Book the court
home.how.items.3.text: The clubs in your city in one list, with the hours still free on the day you picked and what they cost. Pick an hour and go play.
home.how.items.4.title: Play, then enter the score
home.how.items.4.text: Everything else follows: rating, history, leaderboard, statistics.
home.features.title: The parts nobody else builds
home.features.lead: Half the padel apps out there are a calendar with a Join button. Past that point is the reason we built this.
home.features.items.0.title: Matching that explains itself
home.features.items.0.text: Level, interests, court side, age. Under each name it says why this person suits you — instead of just "recommended".
home.features.items.1.title: Your game, analysed
home.features.items.1.text: Which side of the court you are stronger on. Which day and hour you win more often. What happens at one set all. Who you actually play well with. We have not seen this in any other racket-sport app.
home.features.items.2.title: Tournaments at any size
home.features.items.2.text: An evening for four, a draw for thirty-two, a championship that runs for a month. Rotations, seeding and the table are the app's problem.
home.features.items.3.title: A rating you can trust
home.features.items.3.text: Recalculated after every match and adjusted for the level of everyone on court. Next to it you can see how many games stand behind the number, so nobody inflates one with a couple of lucky evenings.
home.features.items.4.title: Marks from the people you played with
home.features.items.4.text: Anonymous and specific: not a score out of five but "strong serve, stamina drops off". They build the chart of your strengths.
home.features.items.5.title: The city's courts in one list
home.features.items.5.text: Free hours, prices, a filter by time of day. Plus an alert when an evening opens up at the venue you wanted.
home.why.title: The comparison, without false modesty
home.why.lead: Clubs are usually choosing between us, an international booking app, and a spreadsheet.
home.faq.title: Frequently asked
home.faq.items.0.question: What does it cost a player?
home.faq.items.0.answer: Playing, finding games, creating them, keeping a rating and entering tournaments is free. There are PRO and MAX subscriptions that open up the deeper analytics and some extras. The court itself you pay for at the venue, and that money is theirs.
home.faq.items.1.question: Which sports?
home.faq.items.1.answer: Padel, tennis, table tennis, badminton, squash and pickleball. Padel is where most of the play is and the tournament formats were built around it. Rating, player matching and statistics work across all six.
home.faq.items.2.question: Do I have to install anything?
home.faq.items.2.answer: No. There is a full web version and a Telegram Mini App with the same account and the same data. The native app is only more convenient for notifications.
home.faq.items.3.question: I am a beginner. Will I be put in with people who wipe the floor with me?
home.faq.items.3.answer: Every game carries a level range and you only see the ones you fit. Beginners are visible to each other. If you have never held a padel racket, read our guide first — it covers the rules and why there are walls.
home.faq.items.4.question: Which cities does it work in?
home.faq.items.4.answer: Games, tournaments, rating and coaches work anywhere there is somebody to play with. Live court availability is connected in Tbilisi so far, and we add cities as clubs come on board.
home.faq.items.5.question: How does a club connect?
home.faq.items.5.answer: Through the form at the bottom of this page. Setup takes about two days: courts, schedule, prices, staff training. The first two months are free.
home.download.title: There is probably a game tonight
home.download.lead: Install it, set your level, look at the feed.
home.clubCta.title: Run a club or a court?
home.clubCta.lead: CRM, online booking, and players who are looking for a court right now. First two months free.

players.faq.title: Player questions
players.faq.items.0.question: Is it really free?
players.faq.items.0.answer: Playing, finding games, creating them, keeping a rating and entering tournaments — yes. There are PRO and MAX subscriptions that open the deeper analytics and some extras. The court you pay for at the venue.
players.faq.items.1.question: I do not have three friends who play.
players.faq.items.1.answer: That is the normal case and the app was built for it. Most games in the feed are posted by people short of one or two players. You join theirs, or post yours and let it fill.
players.faq.items.2.question: Where does my level come from?
players.faq.items.2.answer: It starts from your own guess at sign-up. After that the rating is recalculated after every game, adjusted for the level of everyone on court: beat stronger players and you gain more, lose to weaker ones and you drop further. The first matches move it faster so a newcomer reaches their real level sooner.
players.faq.items.3.question: How much can I trust the rating?
players.faq.items.3.answer: Next to the number you can see how many games stand behind it and whether it has been confirmed by play. A rating someone set for themselves and has not yet backed up is flagged as such and does not enter the city top list. That way the top of the table is people who actually played, not people who typed a seven at sign-up.
players.faq.items.4.question: Who marks my attributes?
players.faq.items.4.answer: Only people you actually played with. Anonymously: you will not see who marked you, and your partner will not know you marked them.
players.faq.items.5.question: What does it run on?
players.faq.items.5.answer: iPhone, Android, any browser, and Telegram as a Mini App. One account, one set of data.

organizers.formats.title: Plenty to choose from
organizers.formats.lead: Americano and Mexicano turn up in every app. What follows is what almost nobody has.
organizers.formats.items.0.title: Americano and Mexicano
organizers.formats.items.0.text: In Americano the partner changes every round on a fixed schedule, so everyone plays with everyone. In Mexicano the next round is drawn from the current table, which keeps games level all evening. Both come in individual and team versions.
organizers.formats.items.1.title: Divisions
organizers.formats.items.1.text: A ladder of championships. The first division is the strongest; at the end of a cycle the best move up and the worst move down. It fits a club that plays with the same crowd every week.
organizers.formats.items.2.title: Groups + playoffs
organizers.formats.items.2.text: The classic. Groups are seeded in a snake by rating so they come out even in strength, then it is knockout.
organizers.formats.items.3.title: Court ladders
organizers.formats.items.3.text: Courts stacked top to bottom, the first one called the Throne. Winners climb, losers drop, and a win on a higher court is worth more. There are versions in fixed pairs and a version where one player leaves the court rather than a pair — there everyone answers for themselves.
organizers.formats.items.4.title: Swiss system
organizers.formats.items.4.text: Each round the opponents are picked to make the match as even as possible while keeping your partners across the event as varied as possible. On equal points whoever drew the stronger opponents ranks higher.
organizers.formats.items.5.title: A championship over several weeks
organizers.formats.items.5.text: A group of four to six pairs, everyone plays everyone, then playoffs. Times are not scheduled: opponents agree between themselves and set the match. The stages have deadlines, and it runs itself from there.
organizers.features.title: The work you stop doing
organizers.features.items.0.title: Draws and rotations
organizers.features.items.0.text: Built from the format and the entry list. Change the number of courts mid-event and the schedule rebuilds around it.
organizers.features.items.1.title: A live table
organizers.features.items.1.text: Scores go in from any phone and the table updates for everyone at once. There is nothing left to argue about.
organizers.features.items.2.title: A reserve list of its own
organizers.features.items.2.text: People who did not get a spot wait in the reserve. Somebody drops out, you move a reserve player into the roster with one tap.
organizers.features.items.3.title: Entry fee as a real field
organizers.features.items.3.text: An amount and a currency, not a line in the description. It shows on the card, works in filters, and payment details attach to the game.
organizers.features.items.4.title: Private games
organizers.features.items.4.text: You decide who gets into the roster and who sees the join code. The game still shows in the feed — hiding it from everyone is rarely what you want.
organizers.features.items.5.title: Notifications instead of your messages
organizers.features.items.5.text: Round starts, court assignments, changes, results. Plus game alerts: a player sets their conditions once and hears about every game that fits.
organizers.steps.title: From idea to final in four steps
organizers.steps.items.0.title: Create the tournament
organizers.steps.items.0.text: Format, date, venue, courts, player limit, level range. Two minutes and the draw structure exists. If the format is unfamiliar, there is a "how do you play this" button right next to its name.
organizers.steps.items.1.title: Fill the field
organizers.steps.items.1.text: Send the link to your regulars, or publish it to the feed so players in your city at the right level register themselves. Anyone who does not fit goes to the reserve.
organizers.steps.items.2.title: Run it from your phone
organizers.steps.items.2.text: Start rounds, enter scores, watch the table. Anything that goes wrong is fixed on the spot.
organizers.steps.items.3.title: See how it went
organizers.steps.items.3.text: Final table, every match on record, updated ratings for everyone, and anonymous feedback from the players.
organizers.faq.title: Organizer questions
organizers.faq.items.0.question: What does running a tournament cost?
organizers.faq.items.0.answer: Creating and running them is free, with no cap on how many. Some of the heavier formats and the deeper audience analytics can sit behind a subscription.
organizers.faq.items.1.question: What is the difference between Americano and Mexicano?
organizers.faq.items.1.answer: In Americano the rotation is fixed in advance: everyone plays with everyone regardless of results. In Mexicano each round is built from the current table, so people near each other in the standings end up on the same court. Americano is the more social one and suits a mixed group; Mexicano keeps games close to the last round and suits a regular club night.
organizers.faq.items.2.question: How many players fit?
organizers.faq.items.2.answer: From four up to a large draw, depending on the format and how many courts you have. The app checks in advance whether your field fits the schedule given your courts and round length.
organizers.faq.items.3.question: A player left in the middle. What now?
organizers.faq.items.3.answer: Replace them mid-event — you choose who steps in and for how many rounds. The rounds the departing player already played stay in the record. No support ticket needed.
organizers.faq.items.4.question: We entered the wrong score. Can it be fixed?
organizers.faq.items.4.answer: Yes. Scores can be corrected, and a result can be deleted outright — every player's rating then returns to what it was before that match and the standings rebuild. A mistakenly pressed "Finish tournament" is undone the same way.
organizers.faq.items.5.question: Do participants need the app?
organizers.faq.items.5.answer: They need an account, which they can create in a browser or in Telegram without installing anything. Without it there is no live table and no result in their rating.

padel.meta.title: What is padel — rules, court, scoring and how to start
padel.meta.description: A plain guide to padel: how the game works, what the court and walls do, how scoring runs, what equipment you need, and how to play your first game.
padel.hero.title: What padel is, and why it took over
padel.hero.lead: Padel is a doubles racket sport played on an enclosed court roughly a third the size of a tennis court, where the walls are part of the game. It is the fastest-growing racket sport in the world, and the reason is simple: a complete beginner can play a real rally in their first hour.
padel.hero.points.0: Always doubles — four players, two per side
padel.hero.points.1: Enclosed court, 20 × 10 metres, glass and mesh walls in play
padel.basics.title: Six things that make padel padel
padel.basics.items.0.title: It is always doubles
padel.basics.items.0.text: Four players, two a side. Singles padel exists on a narrower court but is rare. This is the single biggest reason padel is social: you never play it alone, and you rarely play it with the same three people twice.
padel.basics.items.1.title: The court is enclosed and small
padel.basics.items.1.text: 20 metres by 10, surrounded by glass and metal mesh, with a net across the middle. About a third of a tennis court, which means far less running and far more time near your partner.
padel.basics.items.2.title: The walls are in play
padel.basics.items.2.text: After the ball bounces on your side, it may come off the back or side wall and you can still return it. This is what keeps rallies alive and why points last much longer than in tennis.
padel.basics.items.3.title: The serve is underarm
padel.basics.items.3.text: You bounce the ball and hit it below waist height, diagonally into the opposite service box. There is no serving power advantage, which removes the barrier that keeps beginners out of tennis.
padel.basics.items.4.title: The racket is solid
padel.basics.items.4.text: No strings — a perforated composite blade, shorter than a tennis racket. Less power, more control, and much more forgiving on mishits.
padel.basics.items.5.title: Scoring is borrowed from tennis
padel.basics.items.5.text: 15, 30, 40, game; six games with a two-game margin takes the set; best of three sets takes the match. If you know tennis scoring, you already know padel scoring.
padel.start.title: How to play your first game
padel.start.items.0.title: Do not buy anything yet
padel.start.items.0.text: Almost every club rents rackets, and balls are usually included in the court fee. Wear trainers with a decent grip and sports clothes. Buy a racket after five or six games, when you know whether you actually like it.
padel.start.items.1.title: Find a beginner game, not a beginner court
padel.start.items.1.text: Padel is only fun when the four players are roughly matched. Look for games explicitly marked for beginners rather than booking a court and hoping. In RabbitMatch these are filtered by level by default.
padel.start.items.2.title: Learn three rules and ignore the rest
padel.start.items.2.text: Serve underarm and diagonally. The ball must bounce on your side before it hits a wall. You lose the point if the ball hits the wall on your opponents' side before bouncing on the floor. Everything else you will pick up from the game.
padel.start.items.3.title: Play from the back at first
padel.start.items.3.text: Beginners tend to hug the net and get lobbed. Start further back, let the ball come off the wall, and hit it after it drops. The wall is your friend before it is your problem.
padel.start.items.4.title: Book the next one before you leave
padel.start.items.4.text: The single biggest predictor of whether someone keeps playing padel is whether the second game is already in the calendar. Take a spot in the feed while you are still on court.
padel.vs.title: How it differs from the game everyone compares it to
padel.vs.lead: Both use a net, a court and tennis scoring. Almost everything else is different, and the differences all point the same way — padel is easier to start and harder to dominate.
padel.vs.items.0.title: Court size
padel.vs.items.0.text: Padel: 20 × 10 m, enclosed. Tennis: 23.77 × 10.97 m for doubles, open. Less ground to cover, shorter distances, far kinder on knees.
padel.vs.items.1.title: Racket
padel.vs.items.1.text: Padel uses a solid perforated blade with no strings and no handle length to speak of. Tennis uses a strung frame. The padel racket generates less power and demands less technique to make clean contact.
padel.vs.items.2.title: Serve
padel.vs.items.2.text: Underarm and below the waist in padel — nobody serves aces past you. In tennis the serve is often the whole point. This is the difference that makes a padel beginner competitive on day one.
padel.vs.items.3.title: Walls
padel.vs.items.3.text: Padel balls stay in play off the glass. Tennis balls are out. Rallies in padel run far longer, which is more exercise and more fun for the same hour of court time.
padel.vs.items.4.title: Format
padel.vs.items.4.text: Padel is doubles by default; tennis is commonly singles. Four people per booking splits the court cost and makes the sport inherently social.
padel.vs.items.5.title: Learning curve
padel.vs.items.5.text: Most people can hold a rally in padel within an hour. Tennis usually takes weeks of lessons before a rally is possible at all. Padel's ceiling is still very high — the entry is just much lower.
padel.faq.title: Padel questions
padel.faq.items.0.question: What is padel, in one sentence?
padel.faq.items.0.answer: Padel is a doubles racket sport played on a 20 × 10 metre enclosed court where the glass and mesh walls are part of play, using a solid stringless racket, an underarm serve and tennis scoring.
padel.faq.items.1.question: Is padel the same as pickleball or paddle tennis?
padel.faq.items.1.answer: No. Pickleball is played on a badminton-sized court with a perforated plastic ball and no walls. Paddle tennis is a different American game. Padel is the enclosed-court, glass-walled sport that originated in Mexico in 1969 and spread through Spain and Argentina.
padel.faq.items.2.question: Do I need to be fit or have played tennis before?
padel.faq.items.2.answer: Neither. The court is small, the serve is underarm and the racket is forgiving, so beginners can rally in their first session. Tennis experience helps slightly with timing and hurts slightly with technique — padel rewards placement over power.
padel.faq.items.3.question: How many people do I need?
padel.faq.items.3.answer: Four. That is the main practical barrier to playing padel, and it is why apps that match players by level exist — most games are formed from people who did not previously know each other.
padel.faq.items.4.question: What equipment do I need to start?
padel.faq.items.4.answer: Trainers with grip and sports clothing. Rackets are rented at nearly every club and balls are usually included in the court fee. Wait until you have played several times before buying a racket.
padel.faq.items.5.question: How long does a game last?
padel.faq.items.5.answer: Courts are typically booked in 60 or 90 minute slots. A full best-of-three-sets match takes roughly 90 minutes; a social session usually plays as many games as fit the booking.
padel.faq.items.6.question: How is padel scored?
padel.faq.items.6.answer: Exactly like tennis: points run 15, 30, 40, game. Six games with a margin of two wins a set, and a tie-break is played at 6-6. Matches are best of three sets.
padel.faq.items.7.question: Can the ball hit the wall on the serve?
padel.faq.items.7.answer: The serve must bounce in the diagonal service box first. After that it may touch the side or back wall and remain in play — but if it hits the metal mesh before bouncing on the floor, the serve is a fault.
padel.cta.title: The rules make more sense on a court
padel.cta.lead: Find a beginner game near you and learn the rest in an hour.

players.match.title: Not "recommended" — here is why
players.match.lead: A list of people in your city, sorted by how good a game the two of you would have. Everyone gets their own: a high rating on the other side is not an advantage here, closeness to yours is.
players.match.items.0.title: Level first
players.match.items.0.text: You cannot play with someone from another league however many interests you share. So level weighs more than everything else put together.
players.match.items.1.title: Left looks for right
players.match.items.1.text: Two people used to the same half of the court rarely make a pair. The app takes that into account — and tells you which side each person plays.
players.match.items.2.title: Interests off the court
players.match.items.2.text: A hundred-odd tags from football to board games. Padel is the game you go for coffee after, and shared subjects work about as well as a shared level.
players.match.items.3.title: The line under the name
players.match.items.3.text: "87% level match, plays the left side, shared interests: football, business, board games." Without that line any match list reads as a random order.
players.match.items.4.title: And a nudge once a week
players.match.items.4.text: Only when the match is genuinely strong and you have never played together. Nothing good found, nothing sent.
players.match.items.5.title: Likes and messages
players.match.items.5.text: Like someone's profile. If it is mutual you both hear about it, and you take it to direct messages from there.
players.stats2.title: A breakdown, not one win rate
players.stats2.lead: All of it visible only to you: this is an analysis of your own play, not a public shop window.
players.stats2.items.0.title: Court side
players.stats2.items.0.text: Win rate on the left and on the right. Half of all players have stood on the same side for years without once checking it is the right one.
players.stats2.items.1.title: When you play better
players.stats2.items.1.text: Weekday against time of day. For some people it really is Tuesday evening.
players.stats2.items.2.title: Formats
players.stats2.items.2.text: Different people win Americanos and group-plus-playoff draws. This shows which one you are.
players.stats2.items.3.title: Consistency and deciding sets
players.stats2.items.3.text: How evenly you play, and what happens at one set all. It is immediately obvious whether you fall apart in the closing stages or come alive.
players.stats2.items.4.title: Partners and opponents
players.stats2.items.4.text: Who you win with and who you do not. Sometimes it is not the person you invite most often.
players.stats2.items.5.title: Who you play against
players.stats2.items.5.text: Your opponents by level. If you have spent years beating weaker players your rating will not move, and here you can see why.
players.profile.title: A card worth showing
players.profile.lead: The profile avatar is not a round photo but a card in the style of sports trading cards: gradient, pattern, a big rating, your place in the city. You pick the colour and the pattern, and some of them unlock through play.
players.profile.items.0.title: Your place in the city
players.profile.items.0.text: Computed from games, win rate and rating together. Rating alone will not get you into the top.
players.profile.items.1.title: Medals and achievements
players.profile.items.1.text: Some are awarded automatically from results, some by hand for something particular. Some are permanent, some seasonal.
players.profile.items.2.title: Character and profile fields
players.profile.items.2.text: Gender, age, city, experience, playing hand, court side. These are also what partner matching is built from, so they are worth filling in.
organizers.audience.title: Who comes to your games, in numbers
organizers.audience.lead: A separate tab in your profile: not "how many events you ran" but who turns up to them and whether they come back. Plus an anonymous rating from participants.
organizers.audience.items.0.title: Repeat attendance
organizers.audience.items.0.text: The organizer's number. Everyone comes once; the second time is only the people who enjoyed it.
organizers.audience.items.1.title: Popular formats
organizers.audience.items.1.text: Which formats actually fill up, and which ones you keep running out of habit.
organizers.audience.items.2.title: Average player level
organizers.audience.items.2.text: What level shows up to you. It tells you whether to announce the next one for beginners or the opposite.
organizers.audience.items.3.title: Gender, age and interests
organizers.audience.items.3.text: A portrait of your audience. It hints at what conditions and what times to pick.
organizers.audience.items.4.title: Activity by time of day
organizers.audience.items.4.text: When people actually go out to play. It usually disagrees with when you schedule games.
organizers.audience.items.5.title: Your core players
organizers.audience.items.5.text: The people who come most often. The whole event rests on them, and theirs is the opinion to ask first.
venues.integration.title: The city's clubs in one list
venues.integration.lead: A player opens Courts and sees the venues near them with the hours still free today, the prices, and a filter by time of day. Your venue lands there regardless of what you use now.
venues.integration.items.0.title: We work with your current system
venues.integration.items.0.text: We already integrate with the common booking systems. Tell us what you run and connecting will most likely take a day.
venues.integration.items.1.title: The schedule stays current
venues.integration.items.1.text: Free hours refresh within minutes. Sold time shows as sold, so nobody drives across town to a booked court.
venues.integration.items.2.title: A queue for your evenings
venues.integration.items.2.text: A player subscribes to conditions — a weekday evening, one hour — and hears when such a slot appears. An evening freed by a cancellation goes to a new client instead of going to waste.
venues.integration.items.3.title: Your venue page
venues.integration.items.3.text: Photos, courts with surface and type, amenities, prices, reviews. For a lot of players this is their first look at your club.
pricingPage.subs.title: What PRO and MAX add
pricingPage.subs.lead: A subscription adds depth on top of the free part: a fuller read of your game, partner matching, and alerts that save you an evening of chasing people.
pricingPage.subs.items.0.title: Deeper statistics
pricingPage.subs.items.0.text: A full read of your game — streaks, steadiness, strengths, formats. For an organiser, the audience behind the tournaments: who comes back and what for.
pricingPage.subs.items.1.title: Partner matching
pricingPage.subs.items.1.text: People in your city ranked by compatibility, with the reasoning under each name.
pricingPage.subs.items.2.title: Card styling
pricingPage.subs.items.2.text: Dozens of colours and patterns: some open up through results on court, some through a subscription.
pricingPage.subs.items.3.title: Game and court alerts
pricingPage.subs.items.3.text: A notification for every game that fits your conditions, and for every hour that frees up at your venue.
players.steps.title: Your first game, step by step
players.steps.items.0.title: Sign up
players.steps.items.0.text: Telegram, Apple, Google or email. Through Telegram it takes about thirty seconds and you never invent a password.
players.steps.items.1.title: Set sport, city and level
players.steps.items.1.text: Guess the level. The rating corrects it over your first matches — early on it moves faster, so a newcomer reaches their real place sooner.
players.steps.items.2.title: Fill in the profile
players.steps.items.2.text: Court side, playing hand, age, interests. Dull, but this is exactly what partner matching is built from.
players.steps.items.3.title: Take a spot, or create a game
players.steps.items.3.text: The feed shows who is short of players. Creating your own takes a minute and puts it in front of everyone at the right level.
players.steps.items.4.title: Play and enter the score
players.steps.items.4.text: Rating, history and statistics take care of themselves.
players.traits.title: Where you are strong, according to the people who played with you
players.traits.lead: After a game you can anonymously mark what your partners and opponents are good at. Not a score from one to five — actual attributes: consistency, tactics, serve, the lob, playing off the glass. Those marks build a chart in your profile.
players.traits.items.0.title: Anonymous
players.traits.items.0.text: Otherwise marks like these either never get given, or get given out of politeness.
players.traits.items.1.title: Every sport has its own attributes
players.traits.items.1.text: Padel has the lob and playing off the glass, tennis has the return and topspin, squash has length control. You mark what that game actually contains.
players.traits.items.2.title: Contested parts show up immediately
players.traits.items.2.text: If some people called an attribute a strength and others called it a growth area, it lands right in the middle. That is the part of your game worth thinking about.
organizers.control.title: The tournament runs, and life keeps happening
organizers.control.lead: Somebody pulls a back in round three. The wrong score gets entered. The event gets marked finished a round early. In most services that is a support ticket and a ruined evening. Here it is three taps and you have fixed it yourself.
organizers.control.items.0.title: Swap a player mid-tournament
organizers.control.items.0.text: Who replaces them and for how many rounds is your call. The rounds the departing player already played stay in the record rather than vanishing with them.
organizers.control.items.1.title: Drop somebody into an empty slot
organizers.control.items.1.text: Arrived five minutes after the start — not a problem. The free place is filled straight from the roster.
organizers.control.items.2.title: Correct a score already entered
organizers.control.items.2.text: Typed the wrong number, fix it. The table recomputes immediately for everyone.
organizers.control.items.3.title: Roll a result back
organizers.control.items.3.text: Delete a result and every player's rating returns to what it was before that match, and the standings rebuild. Nothing is left miscounted.
organizers.control.items.4.title: Undo a start or a finish
organizers.control.items.4.text: Hit "Finish" too early — put the tournament back in play and carry on. Started with the wrong line-up — undo the start.
organizers.control.items.5.title: All of it without a support ticket
organizers.control.items.5.text: The organizer owns the tournament. Nobody waits on a chat reply while twelve people stand on court.
illustrationsMisc.hierarchy.caption: A court ladder: win and you climb, lose and you drop. A win on a higher court is worth more, so the top of the ladder is where the real fight is.
illustrationsMisc.card.name: David
illustrationsMisc.card.caption: The player card in your profile: you pick the colour, the pattern and the cut-out photo mode. Some options unlock through play.
coaches.schedule.title: Hours you actually have, not hours someone thinks you have
coaches.schedule.lead: You open the hours you can teach and close the ones you cannot. A student takes a free one and it leaves the grid immediately, so the schedule everyone sees is always the current one.
appShots.gamesList.alt: The games list in the app: today and tomorrow, each card with time, venue, entry fee and level.
appShots.gamesList.caption: Open games near you, with everything you need to decide already on the card.
appShots.courts.alt: The courts tab: a week of dates and, on each venue, the hours still free today.
appShots.courts.caption: A week of courts at a glance, with the free hours already on the card.
appShots.venueBooking.alt: A venue page with a week of dates, a duration switch and the free slots on the courts.
appShots.venueBooking.caption: Pick a day, a duration and an hour — the slots come straight from the club.
appShots.coachProfile.alt: A coach page: price per lesson, what they teach and where they work.
appShots.coachProfile.caption: A coach page answers the only question a student has: can you fix my backhand.
appShots.bestMatch.alt: Players in the city sorted by how good a game you would have, each with the reason underneath.
appShots.bestMatch.caption: Sorted by the game you would get. The reason sits under every name.
appShots.setMatch.alt: A finished match: both pairs, the score by sets and the rating change for each player.
appShots.setMatch.caption: The score goes in, and the rating of all four moves the same evening.
appShots.playerStreak.alt: A statistics card with the current run of results and the best streak.
appShots.playerStreak.caption: Not just how many you won — when it started going well.
appShots.playerStability.alt: A statistics card showing how steady results are and which side of the court works better.
appShots.playerStability.caption: Two players with the same rating play differently. Here you can see how.
appShots.playerTraits.alt: The strengths card: what partners and opponents name as a strength and as a growth area.
appShots.playerTraits.caption: Assessments from the people you actually played with, and they stay anonymous.
appShots.playerCard.alt: A player card with a chosen background, win rate and rating.
appShots.playerCard.caption: The card is the first thing an organiser sees next to your name.
appShots.gameFormats.alt: A donut chart of the formats a player plays most often, with the share of each.
appShots.gameFormats.caption: Which formats you actually play, counted for you.
appShots.winByFormat.alt: Win rate by format, one bar per format, with the number of games behind each.
appShots.winByFormat.caption: The format you win most in is usually the one to build an evening around.
appShots.courtCard.alt: A court card with photo, price from and the hours still free today.
appShots.courtCard.caption: Price and free hours before you tap, not after three screens.
appShots.organizerStats.alt: Organiser statistics: how many players come back and which formats they come back for.
appShots.organizerStats.caption: Which formats bring people back — with the numbers to prove it.
appShots.coachSchedule.alt: A coach editing their own schedule: open hours, booked hours and hours closed off.
appShots.coachSchedule.caption: The coach opens and closes hours themselves, and the grid is always current.
